MARKET.head: Texas High Plains growers struggle as pandemic demand boom turns to buyer caution
MARKET.summ: As Texas wines earn broader recognition, the High Plains growers behind much of that progress are navigating a market correction that could shape the state’s next chapter
takeaways: Texas wineries surged grape purchases during 2020-2023 pandemic sales boom, driving higher prices and aggressive planting; demand then softened and inventories backed up.
Growers now face spot-market buying and fewer multi-year contracts, forcing tiered farming: fully contracted blocks get premium care, uncontracted fruit receives minimal investment.
A March 2025 freeze cut yields across High Plains and Hill Country, potentially resetting supply-demand balance, but several veteran growers are considering retirement or transition.
Younger operators like Connor Wilmeth, vineyard manager at Lahey Vineyards, are pushing eastward distribution and formal contracts with deposit requirements to stabilize relationships.
Despite rising critical recognition, the long-distance system linking High Plains growers to Hill Country wineries depends on trust and planning; market uncertainty now threatens both.

MARKET.head: English estates launch prestige cuvées priced to match premium Champagne
MARKET.summ: Are English prestige cuvées worth prices that rival the top end of Champagne?
takeaways: Nyetimber pioneered England's prestige cuvée concept in 2018 with two sparkling wines priced at £150 and £175, matching premium Champagne positioning.

Chapel Down's Kit's Coty Coeur de Cuvée, Gusbourne's Fifty One Degrees North, Langham's Perpetual Blanc de Blancs, and Squerryes's Patience 2014 have since joined the super-premium segment, mostly priced £100 and above.
Extended lees ageing, typically seven to eight years minimum, and selection from finest vineyard parcels define these releases as markers of quality justifying premium pricing.
English estates increasingly adopt Champagne house strategies: named ranges with heritage narratives, small-batch production, vintage specificity, and collaborations with consultants and winemakers.
The segment reflects growing recognition of English sparkling wine abroad and domestic positioning as equivalent to, rather than alternative to, Champagne's prestige offerings.

MARKET.head: Centre-Loire appellations gain traction as Sancerre prices climb past $40
MARKET.summ: Those interested in French wine are undoubtedly familiar with the Loire Valley, but digging a little deeper, there are many subregions within this expansive viticultural area to get to know. One of them is the Centre-Loire. And although the slightly misleading name suggests it’s the center of France’s lengthy and endlessly...
takeaways: Sancerre Sauvignon Blanc prices have risen to $40, $50 or more, while neighboring Centre-Loire appellations, Pouilly-Fumé, Menetou-Salon, Quincy, Reuilly, Coteaux du Giennois, offer similar quality at $20, $30.

Sancerre is at production capacity with no plans to expand vineyards, creating scarcity as demand remains strong; Chad Stephens, Hawaii sales director for Chambers & Chambers distributor, says he cannot source enough to meet customer demand.
Centre-Loire Sauvignon Blancs share Sancerre's minerality and limestone-flint soils but remain less famous internationally, giving nearby regions a residual sales lift from Sancerre's popularity.

Winemakers across the region now face earlier harvests due to climate change, with August 20 harvests becoming possible, forcing them to experiment with abandoned acidic varieties to preserve freshness.

Pinot Noir from Centre-Loire appellations is gaining attention as quality improves; Matthieu Delaporte, winemaker at Domaine Delaporte in Sancerre, calls the quality-to-price ratio a competitive alternative to Burgundy.

CULTURE.head: Eight Grenache alternatives to pricey Château Rayas across Southern Rhône
CULTURE.summ: In the Southern Rhône Valley’s acclaimed Châteauneuf-du-Pape appellation, Château Rayas both epitomizes the region and stands completely separate from the area’s other revered producers. Like its peers, it gets its powerful personality from the sun-drenched and windswept terroir of the Rhône Valley. But in a region famously...
takeaways: Château Rayas in Châteauneuf-du-Pape commands four-figure prices for its single-varietal Grenache style, rarely matched by peers in a region known for blends.
Delas Frères produces a Grenache-forward Châteauneuf at $63, aged 12 months in large oak then concrete or steel, yielding 10,000 to 12,000 bottles yearly.
Domaine Balme, founded by its namesake at age 23, crafts biodynamic Grenache from vines up to 70 years old, aged in concrete, retailing around $24.
Sébastien Clément's L'Amista estate bottles 100 percent Grenache from 1954 vines using low-intervention biodynamic farming, priced at roughly $30 versus Rayas's premium.
Vieux Télégraphe's La Crau cuvée, rooted in a vineyard planted in 1898, retails for about $136 and offers Grenache-led structure with aging potential comparable to Rayas.

CULTURE.head: Eight sommeliers name Sancerres worth premium pricing
CULTURE.summ: There is perhaps no white grape in the world of wine as beloved by drinkers or as maligned by sommeliers as Sauvignon Blanc. Decades of commercialization and the pursuit of mass-market appeal have flattened many expressions of the grape and in the process disillusioned wine professionals about its potential.
takeaways: Eight US restaurant sommeliers identified Sancerre bottles they believe justify prices above $50, citing minerality, food versatility, and terroir expression over mass-market Sauvignon Blanc.
Vincent Gaudry's biodynamic farming and blending of Sancerre's three soil types drew multiple recommendations, with his 2024 'Le Tournebride' praised at $50 for mouthfeel and pairing range.
Domaine Vacheron's Guigne-Chèvres and Gérard Boulay's offerings from the Chavignol sub-zone were cited for minerality and age-worthiness that distinguish them from flatter commercial expressions.
Sommeliers avoided the $30-$45 price band, viewing those bottles as inflated 2020 pricing without quality gains, preferring either lower entry points or higher-end vineyard selections.
Sancerre's bright acidity, wet stone and grass notes, rooted in flinty and limestone soils, remain the region's anchor despite decades of commercialization flattening much Sauvignon Blanc elsewhere.

CULTURE.head: Decanter World Wine Awards 2026 sees record medal counts across regions
CULTURE.summ: Despite (or perhaps because of ) the headwinds buffeting the wine industry, this year’s Decanter World Wine Awards (DWWA) saw a dramatic uptick in quality. Our DWWA Co-Chair and Decanter Contributing Editor runs his analytical eye over this year’s results, highlights and revelations
takeaways: Decanter World Wine Awards 2026 received 16,631 entries judged by 245 experts, including 106 women and 24 Master Sommeliers, with results announced across multiple medal tiers.
Platinum medals rose to 196 (1.2% of entries), Gold to 924 (5.6%), and Silver to 6,193 (37.2%), each category gaining significantly more medals than 2025.

Cool-climate regions gained ground: Germany's Pfalz won a top Platinum for Weisser Burgunder instead of Riesling; UK's Oxfordshire, Shropshire and Rutland earned first-time Golds; New Zealand took two Best in Show and eight Platinums.
Spain's top-medal count surged 52.4% year-on-year, including debut Platinums from Jumilla, Castilla-La Mancha and Priorat; Texas, Virginia and Washington state earned five Golds apiece.
New World debuts in Best in Show included Frankland River in Australia; Croatia's Hvar and Gascony's Madiran each earned their first Best in Show places.

CULTURE.head: Historic vine-training systems face extinction as labor costs and mechanization advance
CULTURE.summ: As labor costs soar, global wine regions are forced to weigh the high expense of traditional vineyard design against its tourism appeal and climate-adapting benefits
takeaways: Alberata vine training, once common across Italy and widespread near Naples, survives on only a handful of hectares today, replaced by mechanizable systems like Guyot and vertical shoot positioning.

Lanzarote's hoyo system, developed after volcanic eruptions 1730–1736 buried farmland in lapilli ash, now attracts thousands of tourists annually but faces collapse from extreme labor demands; active vineyard area shrank 19 percent between 2000 and 2026.

Alberto González Plasencia, owner of Bodegas Timanfaya in Lanzarote, warns that if hoyos disappear, tourists will stop visiting and wine value will drop; local governments have introduced subsidies to slow decline.

Familia Torres maintains traditional pergola training for Rías Baixas Albariño through specialized machinery for ground work; Juan Glaria of Bodegas Rubicon notes that manual harvesting rules in the DO mean all systems require equal labor at picking.

Bellussera, a 19th-century pergola-alberata hybrid in Veneto, fell from common use after silk industry and subsistence farming collapsed; it now covers 9 percent of Piave DOC but may survive through climate resilience and wine tourism value.

CULTURE.head: Brooklyn housing complex installs 450,000 recycled wine corks as playground surfaces
CULTURE.summ: Wine bottle corks are getting a second lease on life in New York City. Earlier this month, a New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) project in Brooklyn cut the ribbon on newly paved pathways and playground surfaces made of upcycled corks. The first-of-its-kind installation is part of the nonprofit Public Housing Community...
takeaways: Public Housing Community Fund and Cork Collective, an architecture and cork-manufacturing partnership launched in 2024, installed pathways and playgrounds made from 450,000 recycled wine corks at Marlboro Houses in Brooklyn.

Cork Collective sourced corks from NYC restaurants and others, shipped them to Wisconsin for grinding and adhesive mixing, then laid them at the site as a $500,000 portion of a $3.2 million open-space renovation.
Children at Marlboro Houses submitted design mockups that shaped the final layout, partnering with Center for Justice Innovation, The Urban Conga, and the Marlboro Resident Association.

Cork surfaces absorb stormwater, reduce ambient temperature by 20 to 30 percent, and avoid toxic plastic or rubber alternatives; under one percent of 13 billion corks made yearly are recycled globally.
NYCHA chief executive Lisa Bova-Hiatt framed the project as proof that resident-led design and cross-sector partnerships can transform public housing amenities.

SCIENCE.head: Light exposure and soil vigor control green pyrazine aromas in wine grapes
SCIENCE.summ: Understanding the divisive aroma compounds best known for creating green notes like bell pepper and grass in Bordeaux grapes
takeaways: Methoxypyrazines (MPs) are nitrogen-based compounds causing green, herbal, and pepper aromas in wine, most notably in Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, and related varieties.
Light exposure is the primary driver of MP concentration in grapes; shoot removal and leaf plucking increase light on clusters and reduce MPs, while shaded canopies increase them.

Soil type affects MPs indirectly through vigor: well-drained gravel soils produce lower MP grapes, while water-retaining limestone and clay soils encourage vigorous growth and higher MPs in Cabernet Sauvignon.
Rootstock choice influences MP levels by altering vine vigor and canopy density, though whether rootstocks also have direct genetic effects on MPs remains unproven.
Temperature appears to correlate with lower pyrazines in cool-climate wines, but the mechanism remains unclear and may be difficult to separate from light effects.

SCIENCE.head: Disease-resistant hybrid grapes slash fungicide use by up to 80 percent
SCIENCE.summ: Fungus-resistant hybrid grape varieties, known as PIWIs, are evolving through advances in breeding, offering growers new options in a changing climate
takeaways: PIWIs are fungus-resistant hybrid grape varieties bred by crossing American non-vinifera vines with European vinifera, reducing powdery and downy mildew damage without synthetic fungicides.
Modern backcrossing techniques now produce PIWIs containing up to 95 percent vinifera genetic material, preserving wine quality while retaining disease resistance from non-vinifera ancestors.

Rapid genetic testing technology rhAmpSeq, deployed since 2019, lets breeders identify and stack multiple resistance genes with precision, cutting fungicide applications from 8-15 sprays to 2-3 per season.
Germany leads PIWI adoption with 4,000 hectares planted in 2025, up 10 percent annually; Bordeaux University and French breeders are developing ResDur varieties to match regional signatures.

Luxembourg study showed PIWIs delivered twofold economic savings and threefold reduction in environmental impact versus traditional varieties, mainly through lower spraying costs and reduced soil toxicity.

SCIENCE.head: Vineyards deploy netting to cool grape clusters as heat stress intensifies
SCIENCE.summ: Netting is no longer just for hail, it is becoming one of viticulture's most versatile climate adaptation tools
takeaways: Growers in California, Argentina, Italy, and Piedmont are using shade netting in fruit zones to lower cluster temperatures and prevent anthocyanin degradation during heat events, moving beyond traditional bird and hail protection.

A 2022 UC Davis study on Cabernet Sauvignon found shaded clusters had 27 percent more skin anthocyanins than unshaded control during heat stress, because anthocyanins degrade above 35 degrees Celsius.

At Petra estate in Tuscany, 90 percent shade nets reduced Merlot sunburn from 41 percent to 3 percent and lowered cluster temperature from 50 to 40 degrees Celsius, but white or green nets performed better than black.

Luis Reginato, head of viticulture at Catena Zapata in Mendoza, uses light netting to create brief pulses of filtered sunlight rather than continuous direct exposure, balancing phenolic development against heat stress.

Achille Boroli at Boroli estate in Barolo found that netting placement matters critically: nets touching heated fabric can burn grapes, and placement only on sun-facing sides prevents trapping heat around clusters.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Restaurants: Dear Sainte Éloise, Sydney, with three nice wines
NEWSLETTERS.summ: After an afternoon walking around Sydney, I popped into Dear Saint Éloise, which is a wine-focused casual restaurant
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Dear Sainte Éloise in Potts Point, Sydney is a wine-focused casual restaurant with a list emphasizing low-intervention wines and strong Australian and European representation.
Fleet Lichen Pinot Noir 2025 from Gippsland, Victoria: planted 1990 on own roots with clones 115, D5V12, 777; bright, tart cherry fruit with brisk acidity. 93/100.
Domaine Simha Sanskrit Gamay 2025 from Derwent Valley, Tasmania: whole bunch wild ferment, 6 months seasoned demi muid, unfined/unfiltered, 12% alcohol; sappy, bright, chalky structure. 94/100.

Sabi Wabi Nomu Syrah 2025 from Pokolbin, Hunter Valley: two parcels (one direct pressed/used barrel, one whole berry/stainless steel) create low-tannin wine; soft tannins, cherry-strawberry fruit, peppery notes. 92/100.

NEWSLETTERS.head: West Coast Aligoté Shines
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Aligoté is having a moment. The workhorse white grape of Burgundy has spent much of the last half-century better known
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow

NEWSLETTERS.head: Who's Afraid of Volatile Wines?
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine industry's obsession with protecting you from acetic acid
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: EU law limits volatile acidity in wine to 1.2 g/L for reds and 1.08 g/L for whites, established in 1979 and largely unchanged.
Sébastien David (Loire) had 2,000+ bottles destroyed in 2019 for exceeding VA limits; Vizinho Vinhateiro and Pittis faced similar enforcement in 2024-2025.
The US allows 1.4 g/L for red wines (1.7 g/L for super-ripe grapes); EU exceptions now permit up to 2.4 g/L for 18 countries' appellations including Amarone, Madeira, and Tokaji.
Vinegar requires 40 g/L acidity to form; health risk emerges only above 10% concentration, creating a large safety gap between the 1.2 g/L wine limit and actual hazard.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Michelin And The Death Of The Wine Guide
NEWSLETTERS.summ: It was entirely predictable that Michelin’s new venture into wine would trigger huffy French recriminations. Its Wine Selection Burgundy 2026, launched this month, awarded nine producers the top accolade of three grapes, another 20 vignerons two grapes, and 33 one grape. A further 32 were merely “selected”.
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Michelin's Wine Selection Burgundy 2026 awarded nine producers three grapes, 20 two grapes, and 33 one grape, with 32 merely selected.
Domaine Arnoux-Lachaux publicly demanded removal from Michelin's guide despite receiving one grape, claiming they weren't visited and stopped submitting wines years ago.
Michelin rates producers based on vineyard management and consistency rather than individual wines, unlike competitor Guide Hachette des Vins which rates specific cuvées.

Consumer wine guides emerged in the 1970s-1980s with publications like Decanter, Hugh Johnson's Pocket Wine Book, and Parker's Wine Advocate, but print guides became obsolete as the internet provided real-time information.

Michelin's wine venture marks the end of traditional consumer wine guides; future guidance will likely come from AI-driven apps and region-specific digital resources rather than comprehensive printed handbooks.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Notable Releases from Troon Vineyard
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Notes on a Vermentino and two Syrahs, one with some bottle age
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Troon Vineyard released 2025 Vermentino and 2023 Syrah from Oregon's Applegate Valley.
Troon Vineyard farms biodynamic and regenerative organic principles in Grant's Pass at the western end of Applegate Valley.
Troon uses ambient cultures for fermentation, minimal sulfite at bottling, and ages in neutral vessels rather than new oak.
Applegate Valley's alluvial soils, high latitude with long summer days, and cool overnight temperatures from Siskiyou Mountain winds suit Mediterranean grapes.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Q&8 | Wang Yuanzhu Talks Grapes, Grain & Ancient Wine
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Coram Collective 集岩酿造 ranks among the most intriguing projects to pop up in China in recent years. Founded in 2023, with production from 2024, this
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jim Boyce
takeaways: Coram Collective, founded in 2023 with 2024 production, co-ferments rice wine with grape varieties like Chardonnay and Merlot, and innovates huangjiu (yellow wine).
Co-founder Alex Yuanzhu Wang, with a Chinese literature degree and wine importing background, was inspired by a Burgundy winemaker's optimism about Chinese wine's future.
Coram's products are already stocked in over 100 restaurants and bistros across Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and Chengdu since launching last June.
Chardomi blends 80% Chardonnay grapes with 20% glutinous rice through a specialized process: rice undergoes saccharification before co-fermentation with freshly pressed grape juice.
Huangjiu peaks in quality between three and eight years of aging; older isn't always better, and modern styles are fresher and cleaner than historical examples.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A wine of straw
NEWSLETTERS.summ: "Why all the grape drying?" "For something beautiful my boy!"
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: Dessert wine consumption has declined for approximately 75 years, with no expected recovery amid concerns about sugar and alcohol content.
Raül Bobet, co-owner of Ferrer-Bobet in Priorat, Catalunya, released a dessert wine requiring 20 years of aging, reflecting personal passion rather than market demand.

NEWSLETTERS.head: What I Learned at a Conference on Drinking
NEWSLETTERS.summ: From the invention of moderation to the return of temperance
NEWSLETTERS.author: Felicity Carter
takeaways: Drinking studies is an interdisciplinary field treating alcohol as cultural and social practice, not merely a drink or health hazard.
Researching drinking history is extremely difficult because the practice was so ubiquitous that ordinary people's habits were rarely documented.

Ireland's 2018 Public Health (Alcohol) Act introduced minimum unit pricing, supermarket barriers, advertising restrictions, and cancer warning labels, though labels were delayed to September 2028 due to international trade pressure.
The Industrial Revolution shifted the meaning of moderation from avoiding disgraceful drunkenness to maintaining sobriety for economic productivity and workplace reliability.

Alcohol restrictions have historically been used as a form of social control, British colonizers used stereotypes of Irish drunkenness to justify repression, mirroring contemporary public health arguments.
